title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a standardized benchmark to test quantum computers on the graph nodefinding problem using quantum walks and amplitude amplification. It quantifies performance by determining the largest solvable problem size before the success probability drops below a defined threshold. The work provides both theoretical scaling analysis and experimental results on real quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper introduces Quantum WalkScore (QWS) to benchmark the performance of near-term and fault-tolerant quantum computers on the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search).
main_result: QWS provides a scalable, quantitative measure of a quantum computer's ability to solve graph search problems, showing performance drops significantly on current hardware for non-trivial problem sizes.
method: The benchmark combines discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) with quantum amplitude amplification (AA) to estimate the success probability of finding a target node on structured graphs.
model_or_system: The problem is modeled on cycle and 2D-torus graphs, and the evaluation is performed using gate-based quantum processors, specifically citing IBM's Heron and Nighthawk architectures.
key_observables: Success probability ($p$) of finding the target node, and the resulting Quantum WalkScore (QWS).
important_parameters: Problem size defined by $(n, d)$ (qubit count and distance), and circuit parameters like the number of DTQW steps ($	ext{num\_w}$) and AA iterations ($	ext{num\_aa}$).
main_assumptions: The benchmark assumes the ability to execute deep, complex circuits, with hardware limitations causing success probabilities to drop below theoretical thresholds quickly.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graph nodefinding problem on cycle and torus graphs, show the quantum circuit implementation of the DTQW-AA sequence, and plot QWS performance (success probability vs. problem size) across different IBM hardware generations.
paper_structure: The paper reviews existing quantum benchmarking methods, details the QWS protocol using DTQW and AA, presents theoretical scaling laws for circuit depth, and concludes with experimental results comparing performance across various hardware platforms.
why_interesting: The rigorous benchmarking methodology and the focus on application-specific metrics (like graph search success probability) provide a concrete, hardware-agnostic framework for assessing quantum computational utility.
